opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think HELM was a really valuable contribution, and I'd say its biggest strength is the philosophy behind it more than any particular number it produces. The "holistic" part of the name is doing a lot of work. For a while the field had a tendency to collapse model quality into one or two leaderboard scores, usually some flavor of accuracy, and HELM pushed back on that by saying: let's look at many scenarios and many metrics at once. That includes accuracy, but also calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency, and so on, all under fairly standardized conditions so you can actually compare models side by side.

From my perspective, coming from work on algorithmic fairness and privacy, that multi-dimensional framing is exactly right. These properties trade off against each other. A model that's a little more accurate might be worse calibrated or behave less consistently across demographic groups, and if you only report the headline metric, you hide those tradeoffs from the people who have to make deployment decisions. Putting them on the same page forces a more honest conversation.

That said, I'd add a few caveats. First, any benchmark is a snapshot of a particular set of tasks and prompts, and with models being trained on enormous amounts of web data, there's always a concern about contamination and about the field slowly overfitting to whatever's being measured. Second, a lot of the things we care about most, like fairness or safety, are very context-dependent. What counts as a fairness harm in a lending application is different from what it means in a chatbot or a medical setting, so a general-purpose benchmark can tell you something, but it can't substitute for evaluation in your actual use case. And third, these models are increasingly being used interactively and in agentic ways, and static benchmark evaluations don't fully capture how a system behaves when someone is actively probing it or when it's chained into a larger workflow.

So I see HELM as an important piece of infrastructure, almost a baseline of transparency the community should expect, but not the final word. The way I'd put it is that it's a necessary component of responsible evaluation, and it should be complemented by domain-specific testing, adversarial red-teaming, and ongoing monitoring after deployment. Evaluation of these systems is going to have to be continuous rather than a one-time score you report at release.

r001.rationale: It describes HELM as standardized infrastructure for comparing models side by side and as a baseline of transparency the community should expect, conveying an emerging standard for quantitative comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think HELM is a genuinely important effort, and I say that as someone who spends a lot of time worrying about what we're actually measuring when we evaluate these models. The thing Percy Liang and his colleagues got right is the insistence on breadth. Before HELM, the typical pattern was that a lab would pick the handful of benchmarks on which its model looked best, report those, and everyone would nod. HELM says, no, here's a large matrix of scenarios and metrics, and you don't get to opt out of the ones you don't like. That transparency alone changes the incentives.

The other thing I appreciate is that HELM doesn't treat accuracy as the only axis. It explicitly tries to measure calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency. From where I sit, having worked on algorithmic fairness for a long time, that matters, because accuracy is almost never the whole story in deployment. If a model is accurate on average but its errors are concentrated on some subpopulation, or it's confidently wrong in ways a user can't detect, that's a very different artifact than one with the same headline number and better behavior on those dimensions. HELM at least puts those columns in the table so people have to look at them.

Now, the caveats. First, any fixed benchmark becomes a target. Once HELM is a leaderboard, models get tuned, intentionally or through training data contamination, toward it, and the signal degrades over time. That's not a criticism of HELM specifically, it's a basic property of measurement in an adversarial or at least optimizing environment. Second, a lot of the harms we actually care about with these models are contextual and emerge in interaction, in a specific deployment with specific users, and it's very hard to capture that with static prompts and automated scoring. The fairness and toxicity metrics in HELM are useful proxies, but they're proxies, and I'd worry about anyone reading a good score there as a certificate.

So the way I'd put it is that HELM is excellent at telling you what a model can do across a wide range of tasks in a standardized way, and it's a big step up in rigor and openness. But it's an input to evaluation, not the evaluation. The hard part is still the last mile: deciding what matters for your application, who bears the risk if the model fails, and then testing for that directly, ideally with people who are motivated to find the failures rather than confirm the successes. HELM gives you a much better starting point for that conversation than we used to have. It doesn't finish it.

r001.rationale: The response describes HELM as a broad, standardized evaluation framework and mentions a leaderboard, but it does not characterize it as an emerging standard for quantitative comparison of language models.

astra-6.text:
I think HELM is a valuable step toward recognizing that evaluating a language model isn’t a one-dimensional exercise. We’d like to know how accurate it is, but also how robust it is, what kinds of biases it exhibits, whether it produces toxic content, and what resources it takes to run. Those are different dimensions, and doing well on one doesn’t necessarily mean doing well on another.

Having a common framework makes those differences more visible. It lets you compare models under consistent conditions and see tradeoffs that would disappear if you just reported a single performance number.

But I wouldn’t interpret any benchmark as a certification that a model is safe or appropriate for every use. You still have to ask: What is the application? Who is interacting with it? What are the consequences of an error? A broad benchmark can give you useful evidence, but evaluating a particular deployment requires looking closely at that context.

r001.rationale: The response says HELM provides a common framework for comparing models under consistent conditions, but it does not clearly characterize HELM as an emerging standard for quantitative comparison.

sol-6.1.text:
I think HELM is a valuable step toward a broader view of evaluation. With language models, it’s tempting to ask for a single number: How good is this model? But good at what, and under what conditions? Accuracy matters, of course, but so do robustness, fairness, toxicity, and the resources required to get that performance.

The value of a framework like HELM is that it makes those different dimensions explicit and gives us a more systematic way to compare models. You can start to see where a model performs well, where it fails, and where there might be tradeoffs.

But I wouldn’t interpret any benchmark as a certification that a model is safe or appropriate to deploy. You still need to evaluate it in the setting where you’re going to use it, with the people who will be affected by its errors. So I see HELM as an important part of the evaluation infrastructure, rather than the last word on evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response describes HELM as a valuable framework for systematic model comparison, but does not characterize it as an emerging standard.
